question: A project manager's prompt says only "never use the word delay in the status report". Claude complies literally but the reports still alarm the sponsor. Which two revisions would make the instruction work as intended? Select two.
options: A) Say how slipped dates should be reported, such as a revised date and the cause.
B) Explain that the sponsor escalates on schedule language, so Claude applies the intent widely.
C) Ask Claude to confirm that it has understood the instruction before it writes anything.
D) Add the phrase "this is extremely important" directly in front of the existing sentence.
E) Repeat the banned word instruction three times so that Claude treats it as a firm rule.
correct_answers: A) Say how slipped dates should be reported, such as a revised date and the cause.
B) Explain that the sponsor escalates on schedule language, so Claude applies the intent widely.
explanations: Correct. A prohibition alone leaves Claude to guess a substitute. Defining the positive replacement is an independent fix that specifies the desired output rather than the reason for it.
Correct. Supplying the reason turns a single banned word into a general principle, so Claude also handles "slippage", "behind plan" and similar phrasing the way the sponsor needs.
A confirmation step surfaces the same literal reading back to the manager and consumes a turn without improving the specification behind it.
Emphasis phrases do not clarify intent. The word was already avoided, so raising the stakes on an obeyed rule changes nothing about the report.
Repetition adds emphasis, not information. The instruction was already followed; the problem is that following it literally does not achieve the underlying goal.
